newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan hard line stalls banks at HK doorstep.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan hard line stalls banks at HK doorstep.

text.p: Taiwan bankers say the Nationalist island's long rivalry with communist China is frustrating their ambition to open branches in Hong Kong before the British colony's July 1 handover to Beijing.

At least seven Taiwan banks are anxiously awaiting a green light from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, keen to open in the territory in the final weeks before it becomes a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China.

Taiwan bankers interviewed in recent days said the Monetary Authority, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, was moving at what one called a "painfully slow" pace. Most said that reflected Taiwan's political caution and protectionist strategy.
"Basically, we are stuck in the principle of reciprocity," a spokeswoman for Taiwan's United World Chinese Commercial Bank told Reuters by telephone.
"Two years ago we sought the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's approval of our plan to set up a representative office in Hong Kong and we are still on the waiting list," she said.

The problem is simple: Hong Kong generally welcomes just one Taiwan bank for each Hong Kong bank that is approved to open in Taiwan. Since Taipei is extremely wary of Hong Kong banks' mainland ties, such approvals have been slow in coming.
Taipei has banned investments by mainland-controlled firms in Taiwan since 1949, when the communists' civil war victory sent the defeated Nationalists into exile on the island.
Taipei and Beijing are not even on talking terms.
Hong Kong, by contrast, ends 156 years as a British colony on July 1 and becomes a special administrative region of China.

As a result, Hong Kong's powerful banks all operate widely in China and many are owned in part by mainland interests -- a problem in Taiwan, where no Hong Kong bank with 20 percent or more mainland ownership is permitted.
Taiwan's ChinaTrust Commercial Bank opened in Hong Kong in April but said the approval took longer than expected.
"We spent more than three years before finally getting a go-ahead," a ChinaTrust executive said.
ChinaTrust's Hong Kong opening came six months after Taipei approved Hong Kong's Bank of East Asia to become the second Hong Kong bank in Taiwan. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd was the first.
Bank of East Asia vice chairman David Lee has said it took two years to persuade Taipei that the bank's renowned mainland pedigree did not exceed Taiwan's 20 percent limit.
Taiwan's Finance Ministry said the ceiling was set by the cabinet's top China policymaker, the Mainland Affairs Council, and that Hong Kong was not being singled out.
"It applies to all foreign firms, not just those from Hong Kong," said a ministry monetary affairs official.
In cases where mainland shareholdings were not an issue, he said, approvals to open in Taiwan should take only weeks.
Hong Kong had allowed five Taiwan banks to set up branches or offices, and Taiwan's Finance Ministry had authorised seven others to seek Hong Kong approvals, the official said.
It declined to say whether any would obtain their Hong Kong licences before July 1.
Taiwan bankers acknowledged that Hong Kong's imminent shift to Beijing rule heightened their desire to open in the territory, reckoning this would save potential trouble.
Bank Sinopac, one of the 16 new private banks in Taiwan, says it was worried that Hong Kong might gradually tighten rules on Taiwan banks after the July 1 handover.
"That's one practical consideration," a Sinopac spokeswoman told Reuters.

Other bankers called this a secondary consideration that paled in the face of the profits they expect to earn in Hong Kong, which has established itself as the banker to China's reform-driven economic boom.

Because Taiwan still bars all direct contacts with China, Hong Kong has been the primary conduit for the US$30 billion in private Taiwan investment that has flooded the mainland since an unofficial thaw in the late 1980s.
